title: Agricultural land use (von Thünen)
examples: How does the distance from the city affect what crops are grown?
Can you explain why the innermost ring is usually different from the outermost ring?
What factors besides transport cost influence this model?

explain.say: The von Thünen model suggests patterns of land use around a market center.

draw.text: Land Use Rings: Center to Edge

explain.say: The model predicts that land use changes based on the cost of transporting goods.
The innermost ring closest to the city grows high-value, perishable goods.
As you move outward, the land use shifts to lower-value, bulk goods.
In reality, factors like soil quality and government policy also affect land use.
Consider a modern supermarket located in a suburb.

faq.q: Does this model still apply today?
faq.a: The model provides a basic framework, but modern transport and global trade complicate it. It is a useful starting point for understanding spatial patterns.
asks: Can we still use von Thünen's ideas?
What modern factors change this pattern?

faq.q: Why is the center so important in this model?
faq.a: The center represents the primary market, which dictates the highest demand and therefore the highest rent for land. Goods must reach this market easily.
asks: What is the role of the market?
Why is the city the most important point?
How does demand affect land use here?

faq.q: What does 'perishable' mean in this context?
faq.a: Perishable means that goods spoil quickly, like fresh vegetables or dairy products. Because of this, they must be grown very close to the market.
asks: Why must things spoil quickly be near the city?

faq.q: Does transport cost only mean roads?
faq.a: No, transport cost includes all methods of moving goods, such as canals, railways, and even air freight. The cost dictates the feasibility of farming further out.
asks: How does infrastructure affect the model?

faq.q: If a new railway line is built, what happens to the model?
faq.a: A new railway line drastically reduces transport costs across large areas. This would allow more types of farming to exist further away from the central market.
asks: How does better transport change things?

facts: The model assumes a single, central market point for all goods.
The cost of transporting goods increases as distance from the market increases.
High-value, perishable goods are found closest to the market center.
The model suggests a gradient of land use moving outward from the city.

quiz.say: Which type of good would be found in the innermost ring?
quiz.why: Because they are perishable, they must be grown very close to the market to prevent spoilage.

wrong.0: Forestry is generally used in the outermost rings where land use is less intensive.
wrong.1: Grazing is a low-intensity use better suited for the edges of the model.
wrong.3: Wheat is a staple crop that can be stored for long periods, so it is better suited for rings further out.

quiz.say: If transport costs suddenly dropped everywhere, what would be the biggest change?
quiz.show: Land use would spread further out

options.show: Land use would spread further out
options.say: Land use would spread further out

quiz.why: Lower transport costs mean that goods can be economically moved from much greater distances.

wrong.1: Lower costs allow lower-value, bulk goods to become viable further away.
wrong.2: The model is a theoretical framework; it changes, but does not disappear.
wrong.3: Forestry is just one type of use; other crops would benefit from lower costs.

quiz.say: A region has excellent soil but is very far from the major port city. What is most likely?
quiz.why: Distance increases transport costs, making only the most durable and bulk items profitable to transport.

wrong.0: While mixed, the extreme distance usually forces the pattern toward the least perishable goods.
wrong.2: These goods spoil too quickly to justify the high transport cost over long distances.
wrong.3: Intensive farming requires proximity to the market to be profitable.
